title: That Sounds Like Your Friend… But It Could Be AI! #Shorts
description:
A familiar voice on an urgent phone call is not proof of identity. The FBI has warned about criminals using AI-generated audio to impersonate people, while the FTC advises independently calling the person back on a trusted phone number. This original animated Short demonstrates a fictional scam call and three habits: pause, call back using a saved number, and consider a private family verification phrase. Never share one-time login codes. This is an illustrative safety explainer, not a recording of a real person or an endorsement of any product.

Primary sources:
FTC on AI family-emergency voice scams: https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2023/03/scammers-use-ai-enhance-their-family-emergency-schemes
FBI AI-generated impersonation warning: https://www.fbi.gov/investigate/cyber/alerts/2025/senior-us-officials-impersonated-in-malicious-messaging-campaign
FBI generative AI fraud warning: https://www.ic3.gov/psa/2024/psa241203

#AIVoice #Deepfake #ScamAlert #CyberSecurity #TechExplained #Shorts

captions.text: That urgent call sounds exactly like someone you know.
What if it's an AI-cloned voice?
The FBI warns that criminals use AI-generated audio to impersonate public figures and people you trust.
A familiar voice is not proof.
If someone demands money or a login code, treat the urgency as a warning.
Step one: stop and hang up before sending anything.
Step two: call back using a number you've already saved, not one the caller gives you.
Step three: agree on a private family verification phrase, and never share one-time account codes.
AI can imitate voices, but a calm independent check can stop a scam.
Verify the caller, not just the sound.
